title: R' Beroka Chozaah
author: Aharon Hyman
attribution: Model-assisted translation, editorially reviewed; publication authorized by Joshua Waxman.

paragraphs: [Taanit 22a](https://www.sefaria.org/Taanit.22a.4-7) relates that Eliyahu was frequently with him. Once he was standing in the market of Bei Lafat and asked Eliyahu whether there was anyone in the market destined for the world to come. He said to him, “No.” Meanwhile he saw a man wearing black shoes — he said to him, “This one is destined for the world to come.” He ran after him — and asked him to tell him what his deeds were. Meanwhile two brothers came; Eliyahu said to him, “These too are destined for the world to come.”

Hyman says that [Heilprin](https://www.girsology.com/seder-hadorot.html?entry=808&lang=en) took the wording from [Yuchasin](https://www.daat.ac.il/daat/vl/yohasin-zakut/yohasin-zakut08.pdf#page=25). Heilprin reads it as “Rav Beroka said in the name of Rav” and adds, “I did not find it.” He then treats [Beroka Chazua](https://www.girsology.com/seder-hadorot.html?entry=809&lang=en) as a separate entry. With due respect, Hyman argues that this was a mistake: Yuchasin has a single notice for Rav Beroka Chozaah. Hyman reads “R. Beroka” as the short heading and “Rav Beroka Chozaah” as the full name, with “said” in parentheses in his explanation. He says Yuchasin HaShalem has the same reading, with the market designation ר׳ אלישפט.

notes.text: [Taanit 22a:4–7](https://www.sefaria.org/Taanit.22a.4-7) gives the market as Bei Lafat and continues from the man in black shoes to his work and the two brothers. Hyman abridges the narrative.

The [Warsaw text of Heilprin](https://www.girsology.com/seder-hadorot.html?entry=808&lang=he) reads רב ברוקא אמר רב (ל״מ) and gives no source in that entry. The attribution to Yuchasin is Hyman’s. The [1857 London edition of Yuchasin HaShalem, p. 121](https://www.daat.ac.il/daat/vl/yohasin-zakut/yohasin-zakut08.pdf#page=25), prints ר׳ ברוקה: אמ׳ רב ברוקה חוזאה together in one notice. This confirms the wording Hyman discusses. Which copy Heilprin used remains unknown.

The 1857 printing has the market wording ר׳ אלישפט. Taanit has Bei Lafat. The printed wording is retained without identifying a different place or person. The supplied short form Chazua is retained, although the printed Hyman (vol. I, p. 294) has Chozaah there.
